segments.text: Math is the engine that powers artificial intelligence.
But as a user, you don't type equations to get an answer.
You type words.
This interface shows a typical exchange.
You ask a question in plain English.
What's the best Avengers movie?
The AI answers back in clear, complete sentences,
explaining why most people point to end game or infinity war.
The input and the output are entirely text.
Behind the screen, the model can only process numbers.
So how do the words you type turn into the math the machine requires?
A logical first thought is to create a massive dictionary.
You could assign a unique permanent number to every single word in the English language.
You type a word, the computer looks up the number.
That system breaks down almost immediately.
People constantly invent new slang, make typos, and insert emojis.
You would need an endless dictionary to map every possible thing a person might type.
Instead of giving every whole word its own number,
AI uses reusable pieces of text.
These pieces are called tokens.
This diagram shows how a single word breaks down.
The text, unbelievable, goes in.
Yielding three separate tokens.
Unbelie and vowel.
Notice the first piece.
The letters UN start unbelievable, unmatchable, and unusual.
The model reuses this exact piece rather than storing separate entries.
The complete collection of all these reusable pieces forms what is called the models vocabulary.
By mixing and matching a limited set of tokens, the AI can process any word you type without needing an infinite dictionary.
When building an AI, engineers decide exactly how text will be split apart.
They run programs to analyze massive amounts of written text and build this vocabulary.
These vocabularies are large.
Chat GBT holds around 200,000 tokens, and Gemini holds roughly 256,000.
Here is the sequence when you hit send.
Step 1, you type your text.
Step 2, a tokenizer breaks your text into reusable chunks.
Step 3, it finds the matching numerical ID for each chunk.
The tokenizer assigns ID 359 to UN, 32898 to BELIE, and 24694 to VUBL.
Tokenization is strictly a translation layer.
It takes human text and converts it into the precise numerical token IDs the mathematical model needs to function.
When a human reads a word, the understanding is immediate.
If you see the word cat, you instantly think of an animal with fur and whiskers.
This comparison shows how AI starts the process.
The machine does not see fur or whiskers.
It simply takes the word cat and converts it to ID 4719.
That number is just an address pointing to the vocabulary list.
The model process is actual meaning much later.
There are no exceptions to this process.
Every single piece of text you send gets broken down into tokens.
This list shows how the tokenizer handles different inputs.
Basketball splits into two chunks.
Proper names like Chat GBT break into three.
The system also accounts for invisible characters, leading spaces and emojis count as separate tokens.
Even a complex web address breaks down systematically into eight precise chunks.
The tokenizer leaves nothing out.
By assigning IDs to spaces, emojis, and punctuation marks,
it provides the AI with a complete mathematical map of your exact input.
When the AI computes its answer, it does so using math.
That means the raw output it generates consists entirely of numerical token IDs.
To get back to text, the system runs in reverse.
The tokenizer converts that sequence of IDs back into the corresponding text pieces from its vocabulary,
stitching them together.
This final translation layer takes all the complex calculations happening inside the machine
and delivers them back to your screen as a perfectly readable human language response.
Deliberate and clear, words become numbers.
That exact translation process is what allows artificial intelligence to work with your language using math.
